facts.claim: "Grew Apart" is on Donovan Woods' album Without People, released November 6, 2020 on his own Meant Well label.
"Grew Apart" was co-written by Donovan Woods, Travis Wood and Logan Wall.
Without People was produced by James Bunton and vocal producer Todd Clark.
Bunton's credit for the album says he produced everything except "Clean Slate", played some synths, guitars, percussion and bass, and recorded some of it.

The album was recorded remotely during the pandemic. Woods worked from a makeshift studio in his Toronto home and emailed files to Bunton. Backing musicians and collaborators added their parts online from their own homes.
Rolling Stone described "Grew Apart" as the album's first release, a looser, funkier song about someone struggling to hide his real feelings about a breakup.

The Line of Best Fit says the chorus of "Grew Apart" is made up of the sad platitudes men tell each other after a break-up. The article also describes a video of a London-based dancer, Wing Yue Leung, dancing outdoors to the song.
Woods said a listener messaged him that the song nailed the idea that there's no reason for a breakup, you just grew apart.

Woods released a piano version of "Grew Apart" on the March 26, 2021 deluxe edition. His press release says he recorded the song solo and with country artist Logan Mize, and that the two versions together passed 15 million streams.
Woods is a Juno Award-winning Canadian singer-songwriter. He won the 2019 Juno for contemporary roots album for Both Ways, and his songs have been recorded by Tim McGraw and Charles Kelley.

research.lineage: Sources place Woods in Canadian folk and country singer-songwriter tradition, and Without People adds a pop-leaning, sleekly produced sound to that base.

draft:
The tell is the word "man." Tucked at the end of the last platitude in the chorus, "It is what it is, man, it's alright," it tells you exactly who the narrator of **Grew Apart** is talking to: other guys, probably over a drink, probably asking what happened. And what happened, we learn in the verses, is ugly. There were nights she left, texts he received, a lie told "with a straight face." He has the receipts. He just won't use them.

Donovan Woods wrote the song with Travis Wood and Logan Wall, and the chorus is built entirely from things people say in quotation marks: "It's for the best," "We had a good run," "We wanted different things." Each line is reported speech, a script he recites rather than a feeling he has. The Line of Best Fit called them the sad platitudes men tell each other after a breakup, and the song's real trick is how it hollows them out. By the time he lands on the hook, "I'll just tell that we grew apart," the phrase is no longer an explanation. It's a cover story he's choosing, over and over, in public.

Why choose it? The second verse is where the song gets honest, and where it hurts most. He admits he doesn't know why he keeps quiet, then guesses that maybe he hopes it isn't really over. Then he turns on himself: "Am I that weak?" That question doesn't get an answer. The song holds two readings side by side and leaves both standing. Keeping her secrets is decent. It's also a way of keeping the door open. Loyalty and longing look identical from the outside, and he can't tell them apart from the inside either.

Rolling Stone heard it as looser and funkier than Woods' usual fare, and the arrangement plays the same game as the narrator. The groove is relaxed and slightly swung, with a snare on the backbeat, a simple bass line, acoustic guitar, and a clean electric guitar picking out arpeggios. A high harmony shadows Woods' slightly raspy, mid-range voice, and his delivery stays conversational, with a little country in the vowels. Nothing in the sound breaks. It's the musical version of "I don't break."

That sleek, polished finish is the pop sheen Without People laid over Woods' Canadian folk and country songwriting, made remotely during the pandemic from his Toronto home with producer James Bunton. Here the gloss serves the story. Woods later cut a piano version and one with Logan Mize, and together they passed 15 million streams. Plenty of people, it seems, know this script by heart.

The song lets you hear a heartbreak through the exact words someone uses to hide it, so every easy "it's alright" lands like the worst thing he could say.

factCheck.claim: The line "It is what it is, man, it's alright" is the last platitude in the chorus, with "man" at the end of it
factCheck.note: The quote matches the lyrics, but "man" falls in the middle of the line, not at its end. Changed to "Tucked inside."

factCheck.claim: Verses mention nights she left, texts he received, and a lie told "with a straight face"
factCheck.note: Lyrics: "the nights you left," "these texts I received," "told that lie with a straight face." "She" is supported by "She's a good girl."

Quoted platitudes "It's for the best," "We had a good run," "We wanted different things" and the hook "I'll just tell that we grew apart"
The Line of Best Fit called them the sad platitudes men tell each other after a breakup
factCheck.note: The source says the chorus is made up of these platitudes.

factCheck.claim: He admits he doesn't know why he keeps quiet and hopes it isn't really over; "Am I that weak?"
factCheck.note: Matches the lyrics; the reading is interpretation.
